Posted By: Cecilia Jamasmie October 29, 2026
Teck Resources (TSX: TECK.B; NYSE: TECK) beat third-quarter earnings expectations as record copper prices, stronger production and lower costs boosted returns ahead of its planned merger with Anglo American (LSE: AAL).
Profit rose more than fivefold to $1.59 billion (US$1.14 billion), or $3.24 per diluted share, from $281 million, or 57¢, a year earlier, Teck said in its quarterly results on Thursday. Adjusted earnings increased to $1.88 per share from 76¢, exceeding the $1.60 analyst consensus cited by Desjardins.
The results delivered an “earnings beat mainly driven by lower copper cash costs,” Desjardins analyst Bryce Adams wrote on Thursday, pointing to an additional benefit “alongside lower 2026 cost guidance.”
The stronger earnings and reduced cost outlook give Teck a cushion as a strike curbs output at Canada’s largest copper mine. Chinese regulatory approval also remains outstanding for the Anglo American merger, which the companies expect to complete by March.
Teck’s Class B shares rose 1% to $89.01 in Toronto on Thursday morning, valuing the company at about $43.7 billion. The shares have traded between $53.55 and $99.91 over the past year.
Copper performance
Reported profit included a $667-million after-tax reversal of an earlier writedown at Teck’s Trail smelter in British Columbia. Adjusted profit, which excludes that benefit and other items, rose to $923 million from $372 million. Revenue increased 33% to $4.52 billion.
Teck’s copper division generated $1.6 billion in gross profit before depreciation and amortization, more than double the $740 million recorded a year earlier. Copper prices averaged a record $6.40 per lb. during the quarter.
Copper production increased 11% to 115,700 tonnes, with gains across all operations except Carmen de Andacollo in central Chile, where flooding disrupted output.
Quebrada Blanca in northern Chile produced 47,200 tonnes, up from a year earlier but below the preceding quarter’s 55,800 tonnes as severe weather affected operations.
Costs fall
Copper net cash unit costs fell to US$1.77 per lb. from US$2 a year earlier. Lower smelter charges, stronger silver and molybdenum credits and lower unit costs helped drive the improvement, Adams said.
The costs were well below the US$2.27 per lb. consensus estimate, while adjusted earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization of $2.31 billion exceeded the $2.07-billion consensus, he said.
Teck cut its annual copper net cash cost forecast to US$1.80–US$2 per lb. from US$1.85–US$2.20, while maintaining copper production guidance of 455,000–530,000 tonnes.
Operating cash flow reached $1.6 billion. Teck ended September with $6.7 billion in cash and total liquidity of $10.9 billion.
The improved performance comes as about 1,200 United Steelworkers members at Highland Valley Copper in British Columbia began a strike on Oct. 24.
The operation, Canada’s largest copper mine, is undergoing an extension intended to keep it operating until 2046.
Operations continue at reduced capacity, with the production impact dependent on the duration of the strike, Teck said.
Merger outlook
Teck and Anglo American expect to complete their proposed combination within the previously announced window ending in March 2027, subject to outstanding approvals and other closing conditions.
China’s antitrust regulator has sought commitments from Anglo American to maintain copper concentrate supplies to the country as a condition of approval, Reuters reported this month, citing three sources.
The merger is expected to generate US$800 million in recurring annual pre-tax synergies by the end of the fourth year after completion, with about 80% achieved on an annualized basis by the end of the second year, the companies said in a merger update .
Coordinating the neighbouring Collahuasi and Quebrada Blanca operations in Chile could generate an additional US$1.4 billion in average annual underlying EBITDA from 2030 through 2049, the companies estimate. That figure covers 100% of both operations, including partners’ interests.
“These results further demonstrate the strong foundation from which we are advancing toward completion of the planned merger with Anglo American,” Price said.

CPKC reported stronger third-quarter operating income Wednesday, on record revenue and higher volumes.
“Against a pretty dynamic backdrop , I’m pleased with what the team has delivered,” Chief Executive Keith Creel said on an earnings call after the close of markets.“We handled 6% more volume while continuing to improve the performance of the railroad , and more importantly, there is so much more opportunity in front of us.”
Quarterly operating income rose 11%, to $1.06 billion U.S., as revenue increased 15%, to $3 billion. Earnings per share grew 3%, to 74 cents.
The improved performance didn’t extend to the operating ratio, a key indicator of efficiency. The OR was 64.8%, a 1.3-point increase over a year ago as expenses climbed 18% largely due to higher fuel costs.
Volume was up 5% when measured by carloads and containers, or 6% on the basis of revenue ton-miles, which is CPKC’s preferred metric.
The Calgary-based company (NYSE: CP ) set records for domestic and international intermodal volumes, as well as for grain. Grain carloads were up 20%, intermodal was up 9%, and metals, minerals, and consumer products traffic grew 8%. Potash and coal volume each declined 8%. Potash shipments were curtailed due to maintenance at port loading facilities, while mine production issues suppressed coal volume.
International intermodal volume was up 11% and domestic up 7% based on RTMs, Chief Marketing Officer John Brooks said. The railway’s Southeast-Mexico SMX interline service with CSX grew 30% compared to the second quarter.
Excluding coal, CPKC’s third-quarter revenue ton-miles are up 17% since the 2023 Canadian Pacific-Kansas City Southern merger. “That performance, despite a tough macro backdrop, is driven by disciplined commercial execution, self-help initiatives, and strategic share gains,” he said. “And our strong service product network fluidity and available capacity provide the foundation for this growth.”
CPKC’s Canada-Mexico land bridge business — which became a point of emphasis amid trade tensions and U.S. tariffs — are on a pace to reach $427 million U.S. this year, up from $71 million at the time of the CP-KCS merger.
“This is not growth we inherited,” Creel said. “It’s growth that we created, taking a challenge and turning that challenge into an opportunity, creating new markets enabled by this unique North American network.”
The railway announced a new contract with Elk Valley Resources, which operates four metallurgical coal mines in southern British Columbia. CPKC originates all of the coal but currently hands it off to rival Canadian National at Kamloops, B.C., for forwarding to tidewater and export through Vancouver. Under the new five-year deal, CPKC wins back 50% of the Vancouver-bound coal volume, or about 1.5 trains per day, Creel said.
CPKC’s key operational metrics improved, with average train speed up 8% and terminal dwell down 7%, which resulted in car-miles per day improving 10%. Fuel efficiency improved 3%.
The railway’s new locomotives — 170 ET44ACs from Wabtec and SD70ACe-T4s that are beginning to arrive from Progress Rail — are saving on fuel costs and reducing service failures, Chief Operating Officer Mark Redd said.
“The newer locomotives have contributed to more than 35% reduction in our service interruptions on our 100-series trains in Canada, a 10% reduction in interruptions in our Western Canadian grain fleet, while improving fuel efficiency on both services,” he said. The 100-series trains are CPKC’s highest-priority intermodal trains.
CPKC’s safety metrics were mixed for the quarter. The train accident rate improved 60%, but the personal injury rate was up 20% compared to last year’s third quarter. “The increase of the personal injuries does not meet our standard,” Redd said.

Photo: Virgin Galactic
Virgin Galactic, the private space company founded by Sir Richard Branson, conducted its last flight to the edge of space back in 2024, when spacecraft Unity went beyond the Karmann line with people on board. Since then, the company has been hard at work putting together the next generation of spaceships, the so-called Delta class. And its first member, the Apeiron, just conducted its first flight. Well, sort of...
Officially called the Spaceship Apeiron, the vehicle was transported from its assembly location in Arizona to the place it will call home from now on, the Spaceport America base of operations in New Mexico.
The spacecraft didn't go there under its own power, but tucked beneath the wacky aircraft called Eve, which will be used to carry it to launch altitudes when test flights and then commercial operations begin.
Over in New Mexico, Virgin's engineers will begin work on completing avionics software integration and validation, while at the same time prepping the space vehicle for test flights. It's unclear at this point exactly how long that will take, but if all goes according to plan, Spaceship Apeiron should conduct its first customer crew spaceflight in the second quarter of next year.
The trip from Arizona to New Mexico is an important moment for the company, but so is the fact that this is the first time we heard the name of the Delta class ship. Chosen from no less than 276 suggestions received from the global public earlier this year, Apeiron is the ancient Greek word for boundless or infinite.
The Delta class design, although looking pretty similar to the previous one, the Unity, is supposed to allow Virgin Galactic to fly paying customers for a brief period of time to the edge of space much more often than before.
Allowing for mass production, the ship should be able to carry two more passengers than Unity, meaning a total of six (plus two pilots), and should fly up to two times per week. The lifetime of each spacecraft is estimated at some 500 flights.
To build the new Delta class, Virgin Galactic partnered with some of the biggest names in the aerospace industry. Bell Textron , for instance, is responsible for making the ship's unique feathering system, while Qarbon Aerospace was tasked with making the fuselage and wings.
The fleet that will make these spaceflights possible is ongoing, with the static test article and the second Spaceship (which could begin operations in early Q3) construction already underway.
Virgin says the design should allow for a cost profile that's unprecedented in the industry – for the record, Unity tickets cost $750,000 back in the day. As a reminder, the previous design flew a total of 12 missions, seven of which had paying customers on board.

Ferrari now has a successor to the iconic LaFerrari in its portfolio. It’s called the F80, entered production last year, and only 799 units will see the light of day.
Some say it does not look that good, especially when compared to some of its iconic predecessors, but that does not mean that it’s not fast. Because it is. The 0-62 mph (0-100 kph) sprint take just 2.15 seconds, and in 5.75 seconds after taking off, it will reach 124 mph (200 kph). The top speed is 217 mph (350 kph), the spec sheet reveals.
Ferrari’s F80 weighs 3,362 lbs (1,525 kg) dry, and features a twin-turbocharged 3.0-liter V6 engine behind the passenger compartment. The ICE makes 887 hp (900 ps/662 kW) and 627 lb-ft (850 Nm) of torque at 8,750 and 5,500 rpm, respectively, and it’s backed up by a pair of electric motors mounted at the front that generated 282 hp (286 ps/210 kW).
There is also a third electric motor that drives the rear wheels, and it produces 80 hp (81 ps/60 kW). In total, this model has 1,183 hp (1,200 ps/883 kW) available via the right pedal, and that makes it superior to the LaFerrari. The latter came with 949 hp (963 ps/708 kW) in total, including 161 hp (163 ps/120 kW) produced by its electric motor (HY-KERS), and 789 hp (800 ps/588 kW) and 516 lb-ft (700 Nm) of torque developed by the 6.3-liter naturally aspirated V12.
Photo: Instagram | mph Production of the Ferrari LaFerrari spanned between 2013 and 2018. The fixed-roof model was assembled between 2013 and 2016, and the open-top variant (Aperta) came to life from 2016 to 2018. Only 499 Coupes and 210 Apertas saw the light of day in total, which makes this model, which was considered a hypercar back in the day, an automotive unicorn.
However, for such a rare thing, it seems that there are always a few examples looking for new homes on the used car market worldwide. Take the one pictured in the gallery above, for instance, which lives in the United States of America, and has barely seen any action over the years. It is a 2014 model year car, according to the vendor, and at the time of cataloging, it had a mere 431 miles (694 km) under its belt.
This means that you are looking at a brand-new Ferrari LaFerrari , despite being well over a decade old, and chances are that it might retain some of that new car smell. The vendor reminds web surfers how powerful this model is, what powertrain it uses, and also mentions the Rosso Corsa exterior paint finish, which fits the model like a glove, this writer thinks. This example has red brake calipers behind the five-spoke silver alloys, and appears to be in perfect condition overall.
A few images of the interior, which accompany the ad that we will get to in a few moments, reveal the black leather upholstery, as well as plenty of red details on the seats, and red seatbelts. It seems that the pillars, headliner, and part of the steering wheel were wrapped in Alcantara, and if you must know, no, the tuning fairy hasn’t visited this example. And for what it’s worth, we (or I) believe that the cockpit has aged just fine.
Photo: Instagram | mph The same can be said about the exterior, too, because the Ferrari LaFerrari may be quite old in today’s fast-moving automotive world, but it still looks like something that could still be in production. And we can say the same thing about its two biggest rivals from back in the day, namely the Porsche 918 Spyder and the McLaren P1, which made up the so-called “Holy Trinity” of hypercars.
This Ferrari LaFerrari is definitely a collector’s item, and chances are it won’t sit long on the used car market due to the fact that it has barely been driven. Unfortunately, the vendor hasn’t said anything about the title, how many owners it has in the papers, and whether it is available for shipping nationwide, but what it did reveal was the asking price. And you may want to sit down for this one, because it is truly eye-watering.
On average, the LaFerrari Coupe fetches between $5 million and close to $9 million in today’s used car market in the United States of America, and the LaFerrari Aperta, namely the open-top variant, is a lot more expensive, as it tends to go between $7.5 and $11 million. As for the pictured example, its next owner will have to pay close to $10 million. At the time of writing, the modern-classic hypercar had a sticker price of $9,850,000 attached to it.
If you had all the money in the world, would you spend some on this barely-driven Ferrari LaFerrari? For what it’s worth, I find it a bit too pricey, but that does not make it any less cool, does it? View this post on Instagram A post shared by MPH (@mph)

U.S. rail traffic increased 7.8% in the week ended Oct. 24 compared with the same week in 2025, as growth in intermodal shipments outpaced gains in carloads , Association of American Railroads data shows.
Weekly intermodal volume, which includes containers and trailers, rose 11.3%, while carload traffic increased 3.6%. Both measures grew faster than their respective year-to-date rates.
Eight of the 10 carload commodity groups recorded year-over-year increases. Petroleum and petroleum products led percentage growth, rising 15.4%, followed by motor vehicles and parts at 15.3%. Forest products increased 11.7%, and metallic ores and metals gained 11.6%.
Farm products excluding grain, and food fell 3.7%, while grain posted a rare decline at 1.4%.
For the first 42 weeks of 2026, combined U.S. rail traffic increased 3.8% from the same period in 2025. Carloads rose 2.7%, while intermodal traffic was better by 4.7%.
Despite its weekly decline, grain remained the strongest-growing carload commodity group for the year to date, up 10.6%. Metallic ores and metals followed with an 8.6% increase, while petroleum and petroleum products rose 8%. Coal fell by 1.6%, and motor vehicles and parts were unchanged.
Combined traffic on the nine reporting U.S., Canadian and Mexican railroads increased 8% for the week. North American carloads rose 5%, while intermodal volume increased 10.8%, according to the AAR.
Canadian railroads reported weekly carload growth of 7.6% and an intermodal increase of 5.5%. Mexican railroads posted a 12.7% increase in carloads and a 33.4% jump in intermodal traffic.
For the first 42 weeks of the year, total North American rail traffic rose 3.3%. Cumulative traffic increased 1.5% in Canada and 5.2% in Mexico.
Why it matters: Weekly traffic growth continues to outpace the year-to-date rate, led by intermodal shipments.

In addition to canning an Orum-acquired blood cancer candidate last month, Bristol Myers Squibb cut a Prothena-partnered neuro asset in the third quarter. But with sales climbing 7%, the Big Pharma raised its full-year revenue forecast.
Bristol Myers Squibb has shelved two biotech-partnered pipeline candidates after reviewing early data, while also disclosing third quarter results that prompted the pharma to raise its full-year revenue outlook.
The first axed asset, known as BMS-986495 or PRX019, is an investigational monoclonal antibody that BMS licensed from Prothena in May 2024 for $80 million upfront and up to $617 million in biobucks, plus potential royalties. The asset is designed to treat neurodegeneration, though publicly shared details are sparse, with the completed Phase 1 trial conducted among healthy adults.
“Following review of Phase 1 data, we have decided not to advance this program,” a BMS spokesperson told BioSpace in an email. BioSpace has reached out to Prothena about its plans for PRX019 and how the decision will impact its organization.
Other aspects of BMS’ Prothena partnership will continue. The biotech initially teamed up with Celgene in 2018 to develop new neuroscience therapies. After BMS acquired Celgene for $74 billion in 2019, the pharma began working with Prothena on the monoclonal antibody known as moponetug, or PRX005, for Alzheimer’s disease. The tau-targeting candidate has secured fast track designation from the FDA and is currently being evaluated in a Phase 2 trial set to read out in the first half of next year.
“Our neuroscience collaboration with Prothena continues,” the BMS spokesperson said, confirming moponetug’s ongoing development in Alzheimer’s.

In the third quarter, BMS also discontinued an early-stage degrader-antibody conjugate (DAC) picked up from Korean biotech Orum Therapeutics. The pharma ended development of the blood cancer asset, which it acquired in 2023 for $100 million upfront and up to $80 million in milestones, “after reviewing the clinical data for the program,” according to a September regulatory filing from Orum. The decision was made after determining that the overall risk-benefit profile for ORM-6151 doesn’t support further development, the BMS spokesperson said on Thursday.
Stronger sales and high-stakes pipeline readouts
The pipeline cuts come as BMS works to build a new generation of revenue drivers ahead of looming exclusivity losses for PD-1 blockbuster Opdivo and Pfizer-partnered blood thinner Eliquis. Last year, Eliquis brought in $14.4 billion in global sales, while Opdivo secured $10 billion—together accounting for roughly half of BMS’ $48.2 billion total revenue . Analysts have scrutinized BMS’ pipeline plans, with BMO’s senior biopharma analyst Evan Seigerman citing the risky nature of several of the assets BMS has teed up as potential revenue replacements.
But today, the pharma delivered top- and bottom-line beats—3% and 23%, respectively—that “continue to support a better commercial story for Bristol,” Seigerman and colleagues wrote in a Thursday investor note.
BMS’ growth and legacy portfolios both delivered revenue slightly above consensus expectations, with the subcutaneous Opdivo Qvantig beating consensus by 5% on improved convenience, and the legacy products driven by stronger-than-expected revenues from Eliquis at $4.62 billion and Revlimid at $303 million revenue.
For the third quarter, the company’s revenue increased 7% to $13.1 billion, beating a $12.75 billion consensus.
BMS has now raised topline guidance for the full year by 1%, from a range of $49–$50 billion to $49.75–$50.25 billion. However, due to a $1.65 billion acquisition-related hit for the first nine months of the year, expectations for earnings per share dropped from $6.75–$7 to $6.35–$6.55.

Notably, data for milvexian—a Johnson & Johnson–partnered oral Factor XIa inhibitor—in secondary stroke prevention remains on track for this year, BMO wrote. This summer, BMS delayed a Phase 3 readout for the candidate in atrial fibrillation into 2027. The asset is one of three key pipeline programs BMS is pinning its hopes on, alongside schizophrenia medicine Cobenfy and late-stage pulmonary fibrosis candidate admilparant.
Elsewhere in the pipeline, BMS is working to address safety concerns in its autoimmune CAR T program, including a death that was disclosed late last week. The patient had multiple sclerosis and died from septic pneumonia after receiving BMS’ zolacabtagene autoleucel (zola-cel).
The pharma had voluntarily paused some autoimmune trials of zola-cel in August but appears to still be bullish on the CAR T’s potential.
“We truly remain excited about [the] zola-cel program because when we look at the totality of our data, we had 190 patients treated in Phase 1,” BMS Chief Medical Officer Cristian Massacesi said on the investor call. “The overall safety and efficacy profile of this product is truly compelling.
“After an extensive analysis of all our data, we identified that the root cause was a change that we made in the selection and activation of the reagent,” he explained. “We [have] now made the proper adjustment of it, and we are working with authority to restart the clinical program as soon as possible.”

Defence startup Destinus has built more than 1,750 Ruta cruise missiles in Europe and now produces more cruise missiles in a month than Europe did in a year before Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, it told Reuters.
The Dutch-headquartered company said monthly output of its Ruta missile had reached nearly 300 units.
Chief Executive Mikhail Kokorich said he expects Destinus from next year to be able to meet demand across Europe, including Ukraine, for turbojet engines in the roughly 1.5-kilonewton thrust class used in cruise missiles.
He said the company was already producing such engines in series and supplying them both for its own missiles and to other manufacturers.
Ukraine’s missile industry has expanded rapidly during the war, but manufacturers have faced constraints in scaling production of jet-powered weapons, including access to propulsion systems.
Ruta was publicly acknowledged as having been used in combat in October 2025, when Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy said the missile had been employed operationally.
Integration challenge
Kokorich said in an interview that Europe was moving from a production challenge to a military integration challenge as missile inventories expand.
The company told Reuters it had begun production of the larger Ruta Block 2 missile, which is designed to carry a 250-kg payload and travel more than 700 km.
Unlike the current Block 1 version, the missile is designed to be stored, transported and launched from the same container, simplifying logistics for larger stockpiles.
“To have sufficient deterrence, you need to have tens of thousands of missiles,” Kokorich said. “But the main challenge … is that European customers still need to build the military units and logistic capabilities to operate these big numbers of systems.”
He said future missile arsenals would need supporting storage, transport, maintenance and targeting infrastructure, and argued that European militaries would need to rethink how they stockpile and deploy precision-strike weapons.
Kokorich also contrasted Destinus’ China-free supply chain with wartime production in Ukraine, saying access to Chinese suppliers would make manufacturing “cheaper, faster, easier” but that Destinus used no Chinese components.
He also pushed back against a growing focus on very long-range strike weapons, arguing that cheaper missiles with ranges below 1,000 km would account for the bulk of future demand.
“We need missiles which can fly long range and attack long-range targets,” he said. “But we need those missiles that fly shorter and cheaper.”

XPO once again outperformed expectations, driven by higher volumes and stronger pricing that continue to amplify the impact of its operational efficiency initiatives.
XPO ( NYSE: XPO ) reported third-quarter adjusted earnings per share of $1.70, which was 13 cents ahead of the consensus estimate and 63 cents higher year over year. The adjusted EPS number excluded transaction and restructuring costs, among other items.
Consolidated revenue of $2.37 billion was 12% higher y/y but $10 million below analysts’ expectations.
Less-than-truckload revenue increased 17% y/y to $1.47 billion. Revenue was 9% higher excluding fuel surcharges. (Diesel fuel prices were 48% higher y/y in the quarter.)
Table: XPO’s key performance indicators
LTL pricing is moving higher
The revenue increase in LTL was driven by a 5% y/y increase in tonnage and a 12% increase in yield (revenue per hundredweight). The tonnage result stemmed from a 6% increase in daily shipments and a 1% decline in weight per shipment. Yield (ex-fuel) increased 4% y/y, with revenue per shipment (ex-fuel) up 3% y/y.
The company’s freight mix includes more shipments from local accounts (SMBs), which are typically lighter but produce better margins. This customer segment grew by 30% y/y in the quarter. September marked the ninth straight month of expansion for the U.S. manufacturing complex, which is a significant source of LTL freight. Management said a recent survey of its customers showed half of the respondents expect stronger demand in the first half of 2027 versus the second half of 2026.
Tonnage trends in the quarter outperformed normal seasonality.
On a y/y comparison, tonnage was up 5.8% in July, 3.7% in August and 5.4% in September. October tonnage is running 6.5% higher y/y. Tonnage growth is accelerating on a two-year-stacked comparison after turning positive in September (+0.7%) to up 2.7% so far in October. The prior-year comparisons are slightly easier in November and December.
The y/y growth rate for yield (ex-fuel) in the third quarter (+3.6%) was slightly lower than the second quarter (+4.4%). However, the second-quarter yield metric benefitted from a larger decline in weight per shipment (WPS: -1.8% in Q2 vs. -0.7% in Q3), and an increase in length of haul compared to a decline in the third quarter (LOH: +1% in Q2 vs. -1.4% in Q3). (The third quarter had some regional truckload freight in the network, which was a drag on length of haul.)
So far in October, yield (ex-fuel) is 5% higher y/y, with revenue per shipment (ex-fuel) 4% higher. Both metrics are expected to accelerate sequentially and y/y in the fourth quarter as length of haul steps higher.
“We are delivering some of the strongest yield growth in the industry,” said Ali Faghri, XPO’s chief strategy officer, on a call with FreightWaves. “When you normalize for those mix factors—weight per shipment and length of haul—our core pricing accelerated.”
Full-year OR guidance improves again
The unit booked an 80.1% adjusted operating ratio (inverse of operating margin ), which was 260 basis points better y/y and in line with management’s guidance (sub-81%). The OR result was just 20 bps worse than the second quarter , handily outpacing the historical progression. The company normally sees 200 to 250 bps of OR degradation from the second to the third quarter. A variety of pricing and operating efficiency initiatives are driving the improvement.
XPO normally sees 250 bps of margin deterioration from the third to the fourth quarter, implying an 82.6% OR. However, management expects to report a sub-82% adjusted OR in the fourth quarter, which would be at least 250 bps better y/y.
It also raised its full-year margin outlook again. It entered the year guiding to 100 to 150 bps of y/y improvement. The outlook was raised on the second-quarter call in July (to at least 200 bps of improvement) and again on Thursday (to 250 bps or higher). The guide includes a 100-bp headwind from higher incentive comp, which is expected to ease next year.
It estimates it could handle a low-single- to mid-single-digit increase in shipments without adding drivers and workers.
It is carrying 30%-plus excess door capacity currently, following a 15% increase to door count over the past four years. It recently opened terminals in the Phoenix and Kansas City markets, increasing its terminal count to 300 across North America. The new locations, along with AI efficiency initiatives, have resulted in more direct shipping routes (fewer empty miles), more stops per hour and less freight handling.
It has also grown its trailer fleet by more than 30% and tractor fleet by more than 20% over the past four years.
XPO’s European transportation segment reported a 5% y/y increase in revenue to $900 million. Adjusted EBITDA of $48 million was 26% higher y/y. It has grown the sales group at the unit and expects the unit’s EBITDA to “meaningfully accelerate” in the fourth quarter. XPO still plans to sell the business for “the right price.”
The company will host a call at 8:30 a.m. EDT on Thursday to discuss third-quarter results.
Why it matters? XPO is one of a few publicly traded LTL carriers. Its quarterly results provide insight into a subsegment of trucking where few public datasets exist.

A view of the concentrator at the Oyu Tolgoi operation. Credit: Rio Tinto.
Posted By: Northern Miner Staff October 29, 2026
Copper concentrate exports from Rio Tinto ’s (NYSE, LSE, ASX: RIO) Oyu Tolgoi mine in Mongolia have dropped about 70% over the past two weeks because of Chinese border restrictions, the Associated Press reported Thursday.
Daily truck convoys have fallen to about four from 12 to 13, mine operator Oyu Tolgoi LLC told AP. The restrictions affect the crossing between Mongolia’s Gashuunsukhait port and China’s Ganqimaodu port.
The bottleneck threatens to delay sales from a mine that produced 113,500 tonnes of copper in concentrate in the third quarter, up 27% from a year earlier. Oyu Tolgoi accounted for about 56% of Rio’s consolidated copper output during the period, according to the company’s production figures .
The disruption comes as Rio expands underground mining at Oyu Tolgoi, one of its main sources of copper growth. Rio is targeting average annual production of about 500,000 tonnes from the operation’s open pit and underground mine from 2028 through 2036.
Border delays
Mongolian border officials attributed the slowdown to infrastructure and technology upgrades in China, including installation and maintenance of an in-vehicle facial-recognition system for truck drivers, AP reported. The work began in August and could continue until the end of December, the news agency said, citing Mongolian authorities.
The crossing is also where Oyu Tolgoi’s reported sales are measured: Rio records payable metal in concentrate collected by customers at the Mongolia–China border.
The operation produced concentrate containing 312,000 tonnes of copper in the first nine months of 2026, compared with sales of 310,600 tonnes of payable copper. Those figures predate the reported slowdown.
The mine also produced 374,000 oz. of gold in concentrate over the nine months, making the route important for both metals.
Growth engine
Oyu Tolgoi’s copper production rose 29% in the first nine months from a year earlier as underground output increased. The operation was running at an annualized rate of about 450,000 tonnes during the third quarter, Rio said in its Oct. 14 update .
In that update, Rio maintained its group copper production forecast of 800,000 to 870,000 tonnes for this year. The forecast predates the reported border slowdown.
Rio owns 66% of Oyu Tolgoi and manages the operation, while Mongolia’s government holds the remaining 34%. Underground production began in March 2023, supplementing the existing open pit.

Never-Ending Residential Cruise Villa Vie Odyssey Ceases Operations, Kicks Guests Off in Cambodia
19 photos
Photo: Villa Vie Residences (Composite)
They said it wouldn't last, and they were right. The "never-ending residential cruise" Villa Vie Odyssey, which company Villa Vie Residences promised would offer a new model of global living at sea, has has ended. Not with a whimper, but with a bang.
On October 27, Villa Vie Residences (VVR), a Florida-based startup with management ties to another residential cruise that was canceled in 2023 just days before it was supposed to take off, announced they had ceased operations. The Odyssey, the first of a planned series of three cruise ships, would go into dock in Cambodia indefinitely, while management tried to find new financing.
When the announcement came, the Odyssey had been sailing almost non-stop for two whole years, after a departure that itself became a sort of odyssey after repeated delays. The ship carried 203 guests and 156 crew, with all the guests and a big chunk of the crew, disembarked in a cargo port in Cambodia almost forcefully.
The Odyssey was no regular cruise ship, though, and that makes the guests' predicament even bigger. It was a residential cruise ship, one that promised guests either 15+ years of living at sea full time or, conversely, the possibility to book extended, 3.5-year cruises. These cruises would be split into segments, so customers could buy segments, full cruises, or jump the shark and buy a villa to call home for the next 15 years.
Photo: Villa Vie Residences Many of those now stranded in Cambodia either sold their houses and liquidated their businesses or spent all of their savings on the dream of having a home at sea, which is what VVR promised.
A five-year lease of a cabin started at $60,000, while a permanent cabin started at $120,000, but cruise prices were more affordable than with an established cruise liner. To these prices, residents also had to pay a monthly fee (between $3,300 and $9,500) for services like food, drinks, medical, WiFi, housekeeping, and assorted costs.
The official line In a statement to the media, VVR says that exorbitant fuel prices forced the decision, citing $1,800 monthly fuel costs per cabin at the beginning of the year that had ballooned to as much as $8,000, mostly due to the war in Iran. The company says that they've tried everything in their power to cut down costs and thus save fuel for months, including by reducing time spent at sea and spending more time in port.
Photo: Villa Vie Residences They mention that the high fuel costs couldn't and shouldn't fall on the guests, since they would be in no capacity to absorb them either way. This was no easy decision, but it is a necessary one , while the company tries to find financing elsewhere.
"Our focus now is on supporting residents, crew, and employees while we work toward restructuring and recapitalization over the next 60 days. That work is ongoing, and no outcome is assured," VVR says.
Guests disembarked in Cambodia are being offered the proper support to find temporary living arrangements, the company continues. They don't go into specifics, but the general vibe is that they're paying for meals and lodging, which is exactly what they should be doing since those very people called the Odyssey their home by contract.
Photo: Villa Vie Residences The reality: 200+ people kicked out of their home, which happened to be on the ship The reality is… not what VVR would like the world to believe it is. Guests no longer bound by NDAs are taking to social media to offer their own version of events, speaking of poor management and poor planning since the start of the Odyssey, culminating in a heartless email in which they were informed they had less than six hours to gather all their belongings and disembark by 2 P.M.
They have not been offered accommodation, meals, a budget, or even as much as an apology or a proper explanation, Randy Cassingham on ResidentialCruising.com states . They were told to get off the ship and then left to their own devices, as if they were not legal owners of the cabins onboard but clandestine guests ferried illegally across the border.
VVR did reach out with some support, Cassingham says, but it was only after 72 hours after they were kicked off the ship – and then, too, with just a list of local hotels where they would have to pay for lodging themselves.
Photo: Villa Vie Residences Guests are also challenging the official line about rising fuel prices being the main cause. Cassingham, for one, says there was "a cascade of problems" in the months prior to the decision, all of which pointed to poor management at the highest level.
A Ponzi scheme disguised as residential cruise ship? That's the unspoken message you get if you go down the rabbit hole on reddit, Facebook , or even YouTube. VVR has been acting shady from the start, even before the Odyssey set sail after months of delay, even "terminating" a couple of guests on claims of harboring a toxic, negative environment among the residents but in reality silencing them for daring to ask pertinent questions regarding the company's lack of transparency on almost everything.
Photo: Villa Vie Residences Itineraries kept changing, the list of promised amenities changed completely by the time the Odyssey left the original port in Belfast, and there were constant reports about underwhelming conditions onboard, from faulty toilets to flooding, bad food, and cabins ("villas") that looked nothing like the renders with which they were advertised online.
It's true, the Odyssey was never marketed as a luxury residential cruise, but it was billed as "the world's first never-ending residential cruise" (*not true, that would be The World) that would allow you to comfortably live onboard while you traveled the world non-stop . But even by these standards, the old 1993 Fred. Olsen ship Braemar with a new lick of paint and newer furniture, was not prepared for the adventure laid out for it.
Odyssey set sail in October 2024, though the initial start date was set in May of that same year, and problems never seemed to stop. By April 2026, it was clear for many guests that the company was struggling: during a "town hall" meeting, they were asked to raise $3 million for an emergency loan .
Photo: Villa Vie Residences In September 2026, another urgent requests went off on the official communication channels, asking for $360,000 to pay for fuel, or the Odyssey risked being laid up indeterminately. This eventually turned out to be the case, even though some guests are saying that money WAS raised on both occasions.
Ironically, while this was happening, while VVR was having trouble with money, they were announcing expansion plans. Last summer, they announced a new line of high-end residential cruises called Avora Residences, with the flagship called Lumina to be next to launch to water.
Shortly after, they announced a sister ship for the Odyssey, Legacy , which would set sail in 2029. While guests were being disembarked off the Odyssey, VVR was still taking money for reservations on both these new and non-existent ships.
Photo: Villa Vie Residences Current and former residents, as well as casual observers, speculate on the possibility of this being some sort of Ponzi scheme in residential cruise ship disguise. Most cabin owners and guests did not own a stake in the venture but some of the early adopters of this new ways of global living, who also happened to be "influencers" who PR-ed heavily for VVR and the Odyssey and brought in new clients, did. Some tapped out before this month's anti-climatic events.
The story is still unfolding, but even knowing this, the predicted outcome isn't rosy.

1969 Dodge Super Bee Flaunts Rare A12 Package, Sold for $150K
9 photos
Photo: CARFINDER/YouTube
The 426-cubic-inch (7.0-liter) Hemi is arguably Chrysler's most iconic engine from the golden muscle car era. And while the 440-cubic-inch (7.2-liter) doesn't come close in four-barrel format, the six-barrel version is a great alternative. It's also pretty rare.
Although not as scarce as a Hemi in terms of nameplate/model-year production, the 440 Six-Barrel was a short-lived powerplant. The 440 was based on the RB block, itself a raised-block variant of the B engine. The RB architecture debuted in 1959 but did not grow to 440 cubic inches until 1965.
Also known as the 440 Magnum, the performance four-barrel version came with 375 horsepower and 480 pound-feet (651 Nm) of torque on tap. Chrysler introduced the six-barrel mill for the 1969 model year. Topped by a trio of two-barrel Holley carburetors, it produced 390 horsepower and 490 pound-feet (664 Nm) of torque. The latter figure was identical to the Hemi.
The 440-6 was originally offered in only two vehicles, the Dodge Super Bee and Plymouth Road Runner . Both had been introduced as affordable muscle cars the previous year. The engine was actually part of a performance package called the A12. Dedicated to drag racers, it also included heavy-duty cooling, a Dana 60 rear end with 4.10 gears, heavy-duty brakes, and a Hemi-spec suspension setup.
In 1970, Chrysler dropped the A12 package and the six-barrel engine found its way into other B-body vehicles, including the Dodge Charger R/T and the Plymouth GTX. Availability expanded to the then-new E-body cars, the Dodge Challenger and the Plymouth Cuda. The full-size Plymouth Sport Fury GT also got it that year.
But like all high-compression Mopar V8 engines, the six-barrel was discontinued after the 1971 model year. In its short stint on the market, the powerplant found its way into fewer than 14,000 vehicles, including both Dodge and Plymouth nameplates.
The stunning Super Bee you see here is one of those cars. More importantly, it's one of those one-year-only gems that was fitted with the A12 package and not just the 440 Six-Barrel mill. It's one of 1,907 cars built for the 1969 model year and one of only 826 equipped with the four-speed manual transmission.
Finished in the spectacular high-impact Hemi Orange, the Super Bee rocks the correct fiberglass lift-off hood, and it still relies on the numbers-matching drivetrain. The same goes for the Dana rear end.
In fact, this Mopar is still highly original, despite having received a refresh a few years ago. The video below shows the Super Bee sitting pretty at Mecum's Dallas/Fort Worth 2026 auction , where it changed hands for an impressive $151,250 (including the buyer's premium). Luckily, the 440 Six-Barrel engine is also on display. Hit the play button to check it out.

Blue Yonder ’s 2026 Consumer Retail Returns Survey found that 46% of U.S. shoppers who purchased an AI-recommended product returned one within the past year. Products that differed from their descriptions were the leading reason.
What’s Related
The survey found that 24% of U.S. consumers have bought something following an AI recommendation. Among those who returned an AI-recommended purchase, 36% cited a mismatch with the description, while 23% reported an incorrect size or fit.
Those results differ from returns overall, where size or fit led at 42%, followed by products differing from their descriptions at 20%. The findings measure shoppers who returned an item, rather than the percentage of AI-recommended purchases returned.
Product isn't what shopper expected
Blue Yonder CEO Duncan Angove attributed the findings to problems with the product information available to AI shopping tools.
“When what arrives doesn’t match what the shopper expected, it goes back in the box.”
Younger shoppers were more likely to buy through AI recommendations. Adoption reached 43% among Gen Z and 36% among millennials, compared with 19% of Gen X and 9% of baby boomers. Among Gen Z shoppers who bought an AI-recommended product, 56% had returned one.
RELATED STORIES: Nine Ways to Keep Retail Returns From Taking Over the Warehouse | Buy More, Keep Less: Gen Z’s Shopping Habit Tests Retail Returns
Stricter policies can cost retailers and customers
Return policies also influenced where respondents shopped. More than half (51%) chose one retailer over another because it offered a better policy, and 29% stopped shopping with a retailer that tightened its rules in the past year.
Meanwhile, 82% said they would shop less often or stop entirely if a retailer restricted their returns because they returned purchases too frequently.
Shoppers accept alternatives
Nearly two-thirds of U.S. respondents (63%) would not pay a return fee. Free return shipping and fast refunds were their leading priorities.
However, 51% would accept store credit instead of returning an item. Another 55% had been told to keep an unwanted product during the past year, and 67% of that group said the experience made them more likely to shop with the retailer again.
A third-party provider conducted the survey in September 2026 among more than 5,000 consumers in five countries, including 2,000 Americans.

The Bald Mountain mine in Nevada. Credit: Kinross Gold
Posted By: Henry Lazenby October 29, 2026
Two employees of the same contractor died following separate accidents on Sept. 3 at Kinross Gold’s (TSX: K; NYSE: KGC) Bald Mountain gold mine in Nevada, according to preliminary U.S. safety reports.
Newt B. Wakefield, 22, was injured while changing truck-bed liners when rigging broke and a liner struck him, the Mine Safety and Health Administration said in its preliminary notice . He died on Sept. 18 from complications related to his injuries.
Brandon D. Wheatley, 31, a leadman joining pipes, died after a pipe he was underneath slipped off a jack and struck him, according to the agency’s separate account .
Both men worked for TJS Welding of Spring Creek, Nevada. The incidents were unrelated, and company-wide safety stand-downs were held afterwards to reinforce procedures and controls, Kinross said in its quarterly results Wednesday.
The preliminary reports do not represent final determinations of the accidents’ nature or causes, MSHA cautioned.
Difficult quarter
The safety disclosure came as Kinross reported a 59% year-on-year decline in attributable free cash flow to $281.3 million (C$394.8 million) for the third quarter ended Sept. 30 despite higher gold prices. Lower output, rising operating costs and heavier development spending reduced cash generation as the company worked to stabilize La Coipa in Chile and Round Mountain in Nevada.
“We remain on track for our updated guidance, supported by operational improvements at Round Mountain and La Coipa,” CEO Paul Rollinson said in the release.
Kinross shares closed 0.4% weaker in Toronto on Wednesday at C$32.18 apiece, before the results were released after market close.
La Coipa’s quarterly production nearly halved from a year earlier to 29,203 gold-equivalent ounces. The operation processed 691,000 tonnes of ore, down 26%, while gold recovery fell to 62% from 76%. Winter weather disrupted mining and milling, adding to problems with higher copper grades and lower recoveries in some sulphide ore.
Improving weather allowed mining rates and throughput to recover and ore blending to resume towards the quarter’s end. Plant improvements were also helping recoveries, Kinross said.
Guidance cut
Round Mountain produced 27,068 gold-equivalent oz., down 27% from a year earlier, although higher mill grades and recoveries improved output from the second quarter. Lower mining rates had deferred access to higher-grade ore.
Fort Knox in Alaska faced mill maintenance and planned lower grades. Bald Mountain also recorded a planned year-on-year production decline, although output improved from the second quarter as more ore reached the leach pads.
Problems at La Coipa and Round Mountain had already led Kinross to cut its forecasts on Sept. 23 to between 1.84 million and 1.86 million gold-equivalent oz. annually for 2026 and 2027.
Third-quarter attributable output of 424,693 gold-equivalent oz., down 16% year-on-year, closely matched the roughly 425,000 oz. flagged in that update.
Higher spending
Even excluding working-capital movements, adjusted attributable free cash flow declined 41% to $391.4 million.
“Overall, we view 3Q as solid after the guidance update, with results tracking well within the revised ranges and backed by enhanced shareholder capital returns,” Desjardins analyst Bryce Adams wrote in a note late on Wednesday.
Scotiabank analyst Tanya Jakusconek took a neutral view, noting adjusted earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization fell 2% below her estimate because of lower sales. Adjusted earnings per share beat her forecast, but lower depreciation and taxes accounted for the improvement, she said.
Attributable capital spending rose 43% to $439.5 million as work accelerated at Great Bear, Curlew, Redbird and Round Mountain’s stage X development. Sales timing also weighed on free cash flow, Kinross said.
Attributable all-in sustaining costs increased 20% to $1,947 per gold-equivalent ounce sold. Higher energy, contractor and reagent costs, lower production and increased royalties linked to gold prices pushed up operating costs.
Kinross realized an average gold price of $4,249 per oz., up 23%, but revenue slipped 2% to $1.77 billion as fewer ounces were sold. Paracatu in Brazil and Tasiast in Mauritania remained its two lowest-cost operations and supplied more than half of quarterly production.
Project milestones
At Bald Mountain, Kinross poured first gold from Redbird 1 early this month. Redbird 2’s satellite pits are now fully permitted, while the initial leach-pad expansion is nearing completion. Redbird 2 is expected to begin producing in 2028 and extend Bald Mountain’s life into early 2032.
At Great Bear in Ontario, surface construction for advanced exploration is substantially complete and the two underground declines have passed a combined 500 metres. Detailed engineering for the main project is more than 55% complete.
Kinross expects the provincial technical review to finish by year-end, while the federal impact assessment and negotiations with Wabauskang and Lac Seul First Nations continue.
Round Mountain’s stage X development remains scheduled for first production in 2028. Underground development has exceeded 9,600 metres, about 8% ahead of plan, and infill drilling indicates more ounces than expected in the initial mining areas.
At Curlew in Washington state, underground development is ahead of schedule, with more than 3,600 metres completed by Sept. 30. Tailings dewatering plant construction and mill refurbishment are advancing, with first production expected in 2028.
Detailed engineering has begun at Lobo-Marte in Chile, where permitting continues and first production remains targeted for the early 2030s.
Kinross ended September with $2.6 billion in cash and $1.9 billion in net cash. It retained its commitment, increased in September, to return half of this year’s free cash flow to shareholders.

GM Chief Product Officer Sterling Anderson, who ran Tesla’s Autopilot program in 2015 and 2016, says dropping radar for a camera-only self-driving system is “a weird religious stance that ignores physics.”
It’s the bluntest rebuke of Tesla’s vision-only bet yet from someone who helped build the original Autopilot. And it lands while Tesla is pushing camera-only Cybercabs into driverless service in Austin.
Anderson made the comments in an interview with The Verge published October 27, after GM’s technology event in New York the week before. Asked whether GM could eventually move to a vision-only approach like Tesla’s, he didn’t leave much room for interpretation.
“If you scale back to vision-only, physics suggests you’ll be in trouble in certain situations,” Anderson said. He added that radar is so cheap that removing it makes no sense, and that “cameras can’t see through dense fog or measure instantaneous velocity like radar can.”

He also said lidar helps camera systems improve faster when the two are trained together. That’s a direct counter to Tesla’s argument that cameras plus fleet data are all you need.
Not your typical critic
Anderson isn’t a lidar startup CEO talking his book. He led the Model X program at Tesla, then directed Autopilot during its formative years before co-founding self-driving company Aurora. GM hired him as chief product officer in 2025, and Bloomberg reported last year that Mary Barra sees him as a frontrunner to become GM’s next CEO .
His roadmap at GM goes the other way from Tesla’s. The Cadillac Escalade IQ is due to debut GM’s “eyes-off” system in 2028 , with lidar, radar, and cameras.
He took a shot at another Tesla habit in the same interview. Anderson said he avoids “eyes off” marketing language altogether, arguing that a driver-assist system that feels very capable already pushes drivers into complacency. That’s the core problem with selling “Full Self-Driving (Supervised).”
Our reporting backs him up
Tesla started pulling radar from Model 3 and Model Y in May 2021. Tesla Vision launched with limitations : Autosteer capped at 75 mph, a longer minimum following distance, and Smart Summon and Emergency Lane Departure Avoidance disabled at delivery. Ultrasonic sensors went next, in 2022.
The decision wasn’t unanimous inside Tesla. Former employees said engineers tried to convince Elon Musk not to drop radar , and he overruled them. Musk told Electrek at the time that “a very high resolution radar would be better than pure vision, but such a radar does not exist.” We argued that there are plenty of high resolution radars these days.
But the bigger problem is the exact one Anderson named: visibility.
In March, NHTSA upgraded its investigation into FSD in reduced-visibility conditions to an Engineering Analysis covering 3,203,754 vehicles, the last step before a recall. The probe now counts nine crashes, including a pedestrian killed in November 2023. NHTSA found FSD’s camera degradation detection “did not detect common roadway conditions that impaired camera visibility,” including sun glare, fog, and airborne dust, and only alerted drivers right before the crashes.
Radar doesn’t care about sun glare. That’s the point of redundancy.
Electrek’s Take
Anderson is right, and he’s in a better position than almost anyone to say it. He ran Autopilot back when it still used radar.
The vision-only case always rested on a tidy idea: humans drive with two eyes, so cameras and enough AI should do the job. But humans crash in fog and glare too, and the promise was always to be far safer than humans, not just as good. Removing a cheap sensor that directly measures velocity, overruling your own engineers to do it, and ending up with a 3.2-million-vehicle NHTSA investigation into cameras that can’t tell when they’re blind isn’t first-principles engineering. It’s a position Musk staked out in 2019 when he called lidar a “fool’s errand,” and he’s been defending it ever since.
Tesla’s own behavior has drifted anyway. It’s building its own fleet maps after years of mocking them , and its Robotaxi runs inside geofences like everyone else’s. Meanwhile, Waymo, with lidar, radar, and cameras, has logged roughly 271 million rider-only miles. Tesla has about 3 million driverless miles since it started pulling safety monitors in January.

Trek is getting a head start on the competition with the latest version of its Marlin+ electric mountain bike, becoming the first North American bicycle manufacturer to feature Bosch’s newly upgraded Active Line Plus motor.
The updated drive system brings more power, less weight, and a smaller footprint to Trek’s approachable electric mountain bike platform, helping make the Marlin+ 6 Gen 2 an even more compelling option for riders who want a capable e-bike without necessarily stepping up to a full-blown, high-performance electric mountain bike.
The Trek Marlin+ has traditionally occupied an interesting Goldilocks position in the company’s electric mountain bike lineup. It’s designed to offer the versatility of a trail-capable eMTB while remaining practical enough for everyday recreational riding, commuting, and exploring gravel paths.
In other words, it’s the kind of electric mountain bike that doesn’t require you to be an actual mountain biker to enjoy it.
Advertisement - scroll for more content
And the new Bosch motor seems particularly well suited to that mission.
More power without more weight
The biggest upgrade comes courtesy of Bosch’s new-generation Active Line Plus motor, which now offers up to 600 watts of power and 60 Nm of torque.
That’s paired with up to 340% pedal assistance, giving riders a substantial boost when accelerating or tackling climbs.
Despite the improved performance, Bosch has actually managed to shrink the motor. A redesigned two-stage gearbox reduces its volume by 17% while shaving approximately 1.1 lb (0.5 kg) from the previous generation.
The new motor weighs just around 6 lb (2.7 kg), helping manufacturers like Trek build lighter, more streamlined electric bicycles.
Bosch has also focused on improving the riding experience, with updated sensors and software designed to provide smoother, more natural-feeling assistance. Specially machined gears help make the motor virtually silent, while improved sealing and bearings are designed to withstand riding in all weather conditions.
The motor provides pedal assistance up to 20 mph (32 km/h) in the US, making it a Class 1 e-bike without a throttle. With a launch price of US $2,999, it’s also one of the more affordable options in Trek’s lineup.
For a bike like the Marlin+, that combination of moderate weight, smooth assistance, and plenty of usable power could be more important than chasing the enormous torque figures found on increasingly powerful premium eMTBs.
Bosch has more upgrades coming, too
The new motor isn’t the only addition to Bosch’s electric bicycle ecosystem this fall.
The company has also unveiled its new Intuvia 200 display, featuring a 2.4-inch grayscale screen designed to remain readable in bright sunlight. It’s joined by a redesigned LED Controller that’s approximately 65% smaller than the previous LED Remote, offering five thumb-operated buttons and a USB-C charging port.
Bosch is also expanding its theft protection technology with an updated ConnectModule that uses Bluetooth Low Energy alongside GPS and cellular connectivity to help locate stolen e-bikes within a few yards, including in areas where GPS reception is poor.
Perhaps most interesting for long-distance riders is the new PowerTube 720 battery, which packs 720 Wh of capacity into a compact package weighing just 8.6 lb (3.9 kg). Bosch claims up to 115 miles (185 km) of range under favorable conditions on compatible touring e-bikes.
Those additional products are part of Bosch’s broader smart system updates, though Trek hasn’t confirmed which, if any, will be included on the updated Marlin+.
With Bosch supplying drive systems to a large number of e-bike makers worldwide, these upgrades will likely find their way onto plenty of other electric bicycles in the coming months.
But for now, Trek gets the distinction of being first in North America to bring the new Active Line Plus motor to riders.

Alamos Gold's Island Gold mine, about 80 km north of Wawa, Ont. Credit: Alamos Gold
Posted By: Henry Lazenby October 29, 2026
Alamos Gold (TSX: AGI; NYSE: AGI) has pushed back its Island Gold shaft expansion by about a quarter and flagged higher construction costs, delaying a key source of production growth and cost savings in northern Ontario.
Commissioning is now expected to be completed by mid-2027 rather than the first quarter, the company said Wednesday in its quarterly results . The stage 3+ shaft project is expected to run about 5% above its $835-million (C$1.17-billion) budget, implying a total cost of roughly $877 million.
“We view third-quarter results as slightly weaker than expected and note that updates to the 2027 outlook are also a slight negative,” Desjardins mining analyst Bryce Adams wrote in a note late on Wednesday. “On the back of third-quarter operating and financial results, we expect the shares to underperform peers.”
The shaft is meant to replace truck haulage with hoisting ore and waste to surface, allowing Alamos to mine more tonnes at lower costs. Its delay, alongside slower development at Puerto Del Aire in Mexico and continuing constraints at Young-Davidson in Ontario, puts pressure on production and costs into 2027.
Output outlook
Formal guidance for next year has not been updated, but the commentary points to a lower production outlook, Adams said.
BMO Capital Markets analyst Brian Quast lowered his target price to C$70 while retaining an outperform rating. Updates at Island Gold and Puerto Del Aire are likely to weigh on 2027 production guidance, he said.
Alamos shares finished 1.3% stronger in Toronto on Wednesday at C$44.29 apiece, before the results were released after market close. They have traded between C$38.03 and C$75.78 over the past 12 months, giving the company a market capitalization of about C$18.5 billion.
Ground support
Alamos encountered a dyke while excavating underground storage bins for the shaft’s ore and waste handling system. The rock formation requires additional ground support, and the company is also reinforcing the loading pocket and broader handling system, it said.
Underground mining rates are still expected to exceed 2,000 tonnes a day in the first half of next year. However, the increase to 2,400 tonnes a day is now expected in the second half.
The higher project cost reflects inflation and the additional work on the handling system. Alamos had spent about $815 million on the shaft expansion by Sept. 30.
Island Gold and the neighbouring Magino open pit form the Island Gold District near Dubreuilville, about 650 km northwest of Toronto. A separate $542-million district expansion includes doubling Magino’s mill capacity to 20,000 tonnes a day. That work remains scheduled for completion in the first quarter of 2028.
The company expects the expanded district to average 534,000 oz. of gold annually over its first decade starting in 2028, at mine-site all-in sustaining costs of $1,025 per ounce.
Further setbacks
At Puerto Del Aire, within the Mulatos District in Sonora, unexpected ground conditions and contractor performance have slowed underground development. The mill remains on track for completion by mid-2027, but lower mining rates are expected to reduce production below previous plans during the second half of next year.
Young-Davidson is rebuilding access and installing stronger ground support following June seismic events . Alamos expects mining rates to recover gradually through 2027 and 2028, with an updated mine plan to accompany its three-year guidance early next year.
The setbacks come despite record quarterly output of 68,700 oz. from the Island Gold District. Underground mining averaged a record 1,790 tonnes a day, up 15% from the second quarter, while Magino’s mill throughput rose 16% to 10,313 tonnes a day.
The district would need to produce 92,600 oz. in the current quarter, a 35% increase from the third quarter, just to reach the low end of its annual guidance, Adams noted.
Difficult quarter
Group production fell 16% from a year earlier to 119,000 oz., while all-in sustaining costs rose 42% to $1,956 per ounce. Alamos maintained its revised annual guidance of 510,000 to 560,000 oz. at all-in sustaining costs of $1,775 to $1,875 per ounce.
Fourth-quarter output is expected to increase to between 140,000 and 160,000 oz., with higher underground mining rates and grades at Island Gold helping lift production and lower costs, Alamos said.
The near-term setbacks are primarily timing and execution issues, while the longer-term growth outlook remains intact, National Bank Financial analyst Don DeMarco said. He retained an outperform rating and C$81 target price.
The company ended September with $597.4 million in cash and about $1.15 billion in total liquidity. It expects to fund its growth projects internally and received another $160 million in October from last year’s sale of its Turkish projects.
Alamos plans to quantify Puerto Del Aire’s production and cost effects in its updated three-year guidance early next year.
“Through the expansions of the Island Gold District and development of Lynn Lake, we remain on track to nearly double our rate of production to approximately 1 million oz. annually by 2030, at substantially lower costs,” CEO John McCluskey said in the release.

Aerial view of the Omitiomire project area in Namibia. Credit: Appian Capital Advisory.
Posted By: Northern Miner Staff October 29, 2026
Appian Capital Advisory plans to invest about $2 billion (C$2.8 billion) in Africa, even as CEO Michael Scherb warns that unpredictable government policies are pushing mining capital towards Latin America, Reuters reported .
The African allocation forms part of a $5-billion to $7-billion global investment plan over the next 12 to 24 months, Scherb told the news agency on Tuesday.
Morocco, Namibia and Botswana rank among the London-based mining investor’s preferred African jurisdictions, while Ghana, the Ivory Coast, Mauritania and Senegal are being assessed for opportunities, he said.
Appian holds three active investments in Africa, compared with four in Latin America, according to Reuters.
Namibian copper
Appian acquired a 95% interest in Namibia’s Omitiomire copper project in May, the firm said in its acquisition announcement . Developing the asset is expected to require more than $400 million.
The project, about 140 km northeast of Windhoek, could produce 26,000 to 30,000 tonnes of copper annually over 16 years, according to Appian’s current portfolio page . The remaining 5% belongs to the Craton Foundation Trust, a Namibian community trust.
Appian’s development plan centres on a switch from leaching to flotation and changes to mine scheduling. A controlling interest in the Rosh Pinah zinc mine, acquired in 2023, provides an operating base in Namibia.
Latin American expansion
Appian opened regional headquarters in São Paulo in April to support investment across Brazil, Peru, Chile, Argentina and Mexico.
The firm had made 13 investments in Latin America since 2016 and held four projects in Brazil at the time, according to its office announcement.
Appian’s financing capacity also includes a partnership launched last year with the World Bank Group’s International Finance Corporation (IFC). The fund is targeting up to $1 billion for mining and related investments in emerging markets, focusing on Africa and Latin America.
IFC committed an initial $100 million, with additional capital to be raised through its asset management arm. IFC will invest alongside Appian’s existing and future funds through equity, credit and royalties.
The partners agreed to make the fund’s first investment in Atlantic Nickel’s Santa Rita operation in Brazil to support an underground expansion. Early development work began in March, with more than 600 metres of tunnels excavated by Appian’s Oct. 5 update .

Every career has a story. In Leadership Lessons , supply chain leaders reflect on the experiences that shaped who they are and how they lead.
Long before Jonathan Scherr was helping lead a supply chain technology company, he spent Saturday nights as an event DJ outside Boston, working weddings and bar mitzvahs.
The job meant walking into a room full of strangers and helping them celebrate. When something went wrong, he had to stay upbeat and fix it fast.
More Leadership Lessons
Lindsay Azim, Gartner
Steve Liou, CEO of Clarium
Jackie Wu, Corvus Robotics
Peter Bollinger, CEO of EPG
Peter Bennett, Cardinal Health
View all Leadership Lessons stories
“As a first job it was a crash course on thinking on my feet. Constantly had to read a room, course correct when things weren't working, and deal with people when emotions were running high.”
Now chief strategy and operations officer at project44 , Scherr works to bring the same optimism and solution orientation to some of the most complex problems facing customers and their supply chain operations. Another principle guides how he leads: “Just show up is a pretty powerful thesis, first and foremost.”
Being there for people has followed him through a career spanning finance, education , technology , and housing. Along the way, he has learned that showing up also means taking responsibility, especially when something goes wrong.
Curiosity starts at home
Scherr grew up in Newton, Massachusetts, the younger of two brothers. His mother spent decades working in Boston public schools as a speech and language pathologist, while his father moved from education into construction and real estate.
Education mattered at home, but so did asking questions. Dinner conversations encouraged the brothers to discuss what they had learned and keep asking why.
Scherr loved musical theater, played sports, and became editor-in-chief of his high school newspaper.
At Dartmouth, he initially thought he would become a doctor, following in the footsteps of an uncle who was a surgeon. During the college’s shopping period, he sat in on the first organic chemistry class and walked out within 30 minutes.
An introductory economics class offered something more appealing: a way to study why people make decisions. He became especially interested in development economics and how household choices could improve someone’s financial prospects or keep a family in poverty.
It laid the foundation for a deep interest in using data to understand the world differently and shed light on how organizations should operate to do things better. Everything he's focused on since has been grounded in that foundation
At 20, he took a semester off to work with a nonprofit in Tanzania providing care to people with HIV and AIDS. Drawing on emergency medical training from Dartmouth’s ski patrol, he helped with home-based health care and hospice work.
The experience brought his studies to life. It also led him to question nonprofits as a way to address those problems, given the waste and inefficiency he observed.
RELATED STORIES: project44 Creates Standalone Business for Logistics Providers | project44 Launches AI Tool to Help Companies Make Better Decisions
Leaving the comfortable path
Scherr’s early finance work included commercial mortgage-backed securities at Morgan Stanley as the mortgage crisis was beginning. He later worked in private equity, investing in software and technology businesses. His first investment assignment involved Accellos, a supply chain software company that later merged with HighJump, giving him an early connection to the industry he would eventually return to at project44.
He could see a comfortable career ahead. Then an episode of The Colbert Report sent him in another direction.
A Harvard economist appeared on the show to discuss research on improving outcomes in high-poverty U.S. communities, particularly through education. Scherr reached out and eventually left finance to work alongside him, helping turn the research into a nonprofit that works with schools.
Scherr helped found Blueprint Schools Network as its chief operating officer. The work connected his interest in data with education issues he had heard his mother discuss for years and introduced him to personalized learning.
He went on to Harvard Business School and the Harvard Kennedy School, advised education technology company AltSchool, and worked at financial technology company CircleUp. Later, he co-founded and led Juno, which sought to simplify how housing was designed and built.
At Juno, Scherr teamed up with a former Apple executive who spent about 20 years as the company's chief architect for its stores. The aim was to make building housing more repeatable, with consistent components and a simpler process for bringing a project from design to construction.
It meant working well beyond software. Components had to be designed and sourced , so the team had to build a supply chain around them. They also had to work with contractors and arrange financing through lenders and investors.
“It’s a fundamentally different puzzle than just writing software,” he says. For Scherr, the appeal was tackling a practical problem that could improve access to housing.
“I want my team to be 1% better every day because the compounding of that is massive.”
Across education, technology, and housing, Scherr kept returning to the same idea of how data could help solve complicated, real-world problems. While the industries changed, his interest in turning information into better decisions remained constant. That thinking eventually drew him to project44, where years of accumulated supply chain data created an entirely new opportunity with AI . Scherr began advising project44 in August 2017 and took a more hands-on role in fall 2024, before becoming chief strategy and operations officer in March 2025.
“I was very much excited about a business that didn’t exist yet,” Scherr says, recalling his initial involvement in 2017. The company was building connections between sources of supply chain information, and he believed the data it gathered could become the basis for something much bigger.
By 2024, he felt that opportunity had arrived. After years of building a vast supply chain data network, project44 was positioned to capitalize on advances in AI. Scherr stepped into a more active leadership role with a central mandate: accelerate the company’s AI strategy and turn its data advantage into technology that could help customers make better supply chain decisions.
That focus helped shape project44’s evolution toward using AI to help customers anticipate disruptions , use insights, make decisions and take action.
Today, Scherr says, companies with complex supply chain challenges use project44’s platform to reduce friction and bias in their work. Its data foundation gives customers reliable information for AI, whether they use project44’s agentic platform or draw on its data for AI applications elsewhere.
Responsibility moves up
Scherr’s “just show up” approach to leadership means frequent travel to meet with project44’s global team, customers and prospective customers. At the time of the interview, he had traveled to India nine times to meet colleagues in Bangalore, often for just two or three days. He says the office has more than 250 people, roughly half the company’s headcount, so time there is important for understanding and developing the team and ensuring the company delivers on its promises to customers.
“It’s really powerful when you show up,” he says of spending time with that team. With two young children at home, the travel also requires him to be especially present when he returns.
He keeps a sign beside his desk that reads “1% better.” It reminds him to consider each day how he and his team have improved as people, contributors or teammates.
“I want my team to be 1% better every day because the compounding of that is massive,” he says. His point is that small daily gains build on one another, while small declines accumulate in the other direction.
Another expectation is more pointed: “Never be as surprised as me.” When a direct report brings him an issue and says, “I’m as surprised as you,” Scherr responds, “You don’t get to be.”
Surprises happen when a company moves quickly, but managers should understand and take responsibility for their areas. He holds himself to the same standard as the CEO. For Scherr, wins are earned by the front lines, while losses are owned at the top.
