source_document.body:
When a shipper puts an LTL lane out to bid, price is the number everyone can compare in five minutes. Price, however, doesn’t say much about what happens six months into the contract. A rate quote doesn’t indicate whether a shipment arrives on the dock when it’s supposed to, whether the weight matches the bill of lading , or whether a claim gets resolved in two weeks or two months. Those costs simply show up in a shipper’s bottom line in the form of detention charges, rebooked appointments, and customer service hours.
The Mastio & Company LTL Carrier Customer Value & Loyalty Study is one of the best resources for quantifying what happens after the contract goes into effect. Now in its third decade, the survey interviews more than 1,600 shippers directly and scores national LTL carriers across 28 performance attributes. It’s one of the few datasets shippers can use to parse out marketing language from measurable performance.
What’s Measured
Mastio’s methodology does not rely on a self-reported scorecard, and it isn’t built from carrier marketing claims. Each year, researchers conduct detailed interviews with shipping decision-makers (more than 1,600 of them for the 2026 edition) and collect thousands of additional data points from open-ended questions about specific carriers. The result is a grade across 28 attributes that roughly sort into four groups.
Operational performance covers the fundamentals: on-time pickup and delivery, transit time consistency, and whether a shipment arrives without damage or shortages. Service quality covers the human side, including how responsive a carrier’s team is, how proactively it communicates when something goes wrong, and how professional its drivers are at the dock. A third group covers the business mechanics shippers feel on every invoice: billing accuracy, weighing precision, accessorial pricing, and overall ease of doing business. The last layer is loyalty; i.e., whether shippers believe a carrier has earned their repeat business and would recommend it to a peer, which Mastio has found correlates with outsized revenue growth over time.
The study goes beyond a one-dimensional ranking system, and it’s not a simple popularity contest or trophy. It acts as a detailed breakdown of carrier performance and customer experience.
One Strength Isn’t the Only Strategy
No carrier typically wins all 28 categories. The attributes measure genuinely different things, and a carrier built to win on price often isn’t the same carrier built to win on claims prevention or proactive communication. That’s useful information, but only if a shipper knows which categories matter most to their own operation.
If you’re a retailer who moves time-sensitive inventory into stores ahead of a promotional window, you probably care more about on-time delivery and transit consistency than about accessorial pricing. If you’re a manufacturer and you ship oversized freight to a narrow set of industrial customers, you might weigh damage prevention and billing accuracy more heavily, since one mis-rated invoice or damaged pallet can cost more than a year of rate savings. If you’re a high-volume shipper and you juggle multiple carriers, you may care more about ease of doing business and visibility.
The goal isn’t to find the carrier that wins the most categories overall. It’s to find the carrier whose performance aligns with what matters most to a specific supply chain. There are typically a handful of attributes where consistency has an outsized effect on cost and customer experience, whether that’s transit reliability on a tight production schedule or billing accuracy across thousands of monthly invoices.
Old Dominion Freight Line’s Consistent Results
Old Dominion Freight Line ’s 2026 Mastio results are a useful illustration of what breadth across categories looks like in practice. The carrier was named the #1 National LTL Carrier for Quality for the 17th consecutive year and ranked first in 24 of the study’s 28 attributes, based on responses from more than 1,600 shippers surveyed this year.
The headline ranking isn’t the whole story as it pertains to shippers, though. If you’re evaluating the data, you need to see where those 24 wins land. They include categories tied directly to operational risk, like on-time delivery and damage and shortage prevention; alongside categories tied to cost predictability, like billing accuracy and ease of doing business; and categories tied to day-to-day account management, like timely customer service and carrier trustworthiness. That’s a carrier scoring well across the operational, financial, and relationship dimensions of the study at once, rather than leaning on strength in one area to offset weakness in another.
“This award is very important to us because it is selected by shippers,” Old Dominion President and CEO Marty Freeman said of the result. “It shapes how we focus our strategy. From strategic investments to our culture, it is all built around serving our customers.”
Mastio & Company President Kevin Huntsman, whose firm runs the independent survey, called the streak “a particularly impressive accomplishment” given how much the carrier landscape has shifted over nearly two decades.
If you’re building a scorecard, multi-category consistency is itself a data point that suggests performance across a range of conditions, not just the ones a single rate quote can capture.
Consistency Is the Important Signal
A 17-year win streak over a time period in which freight shipping has changed substantially is a track record that’s difficult to overstate. Not only have conditions changed drastically over the past two decades, but so have consumer expectations.
Each year’s Mastio results show a carrier exactly where shippers think it’s falling short, and carriers that take the study seriously use that feedback to fix those specific weak spots before the next year’s survey. The relevant information for Old Dominion Freight Line has been less about any single year’s score and more about whether improvements are made in areas that matter most to shippers.
“Our business strategy is focused on customer service,” says Chip Overbey, Senior Vice President, Strategic Planning at Old Dominion Freight Line. “When we look at Mastio, we recognize it outlines the key attributes our customers actually care about. If we know what our customers want, we then have to ask ourselves what we need to do to ensure we’re the best at delivering what they’re looking for. And that’s exactly what we’ve done. It hasn’t happened overnight, but we’ve stayed focused on chipping away at it and continue to do so year after year.”
That’s a different kind of evidence than a single award cycle provides. A carrier that jumps to the top of one year’s survey could be having an unusually good year due to a fluke in the market, or could be benefiting from a competitor’s misfortunes. A carrier with close to two decades of sustained, broad-category performance has had to keep closing gaps as shipper expectations shift around digital visibility, accessorial transparency, or whatever attribute shippers start weighting more heavily next.
Those kinds of consistencies are evidence of an operation that’s built to keep responding to what shippers are saying year-to-year.
Building Your Own Scorecard
The practical takeaway, if you’re evaluating LTL carriers, is that Mastio gives shippers the opportunity to pull the attribute-level data, identify the four or five categories that matter most to a specific supply chain’s priorities, and compare carriers against those specifically.
For a time-sensitive operation, that likely means weighting on-time delivery and transit consistency above everything else. For an operation with thin margins on accessorials, it means scrutinizing billing accuracy and ease of doing business. For an operation managing dozens of lanes with a small team, it means weighting responsiveness and the digital tools that reduce manual follow-up.
If you want to see how a 17-year streak breaks down, category by category, rather than taking the headline ranking at its word, Old Dominion Freight Lines’s results are published in detail on its Mastio award landing page .

By Angelo Mathais India correspondent
29 October 2026
Intra-Asia and Middle East short-haul trades are seen to be the most sought-after launch pad or entry point for aspiring container shipping entrepreneurs, as the industry becomes more competitive and challenging in an environment of ever-growing trade volatility.
The ‘newest kid on the block’ is Jade Pacific Line (JPL), a company established by a cohort of former executives of SeaLead Shipping, which ceased operations earlier this year and in liquidation, the victim of US sanctions action over its alleged links to Iran.
JPL was incorporated as a Singapore-based entity in April with former SeaLead chief commercial office Doreen Yeo named as chief executive, according to available information.
The new operator has announced the launch of a shuttle loop connecting India and the Red Sea, injecting more capacity into a trade that has already been a target for opportunistic carriers.
While the exact service specifics, like capacity and sailing frequency, have not been disclosed officially, The Loadstar understands the port rotation will be Mundra-Nhava Sheva-Karachi-Sokhna-Mundra.
The 1,118 teu Medkon Sia is said to be the lone vessel deployed on the loop. It had its inaugural call at JNPA on 4 October and is expected to make its next call at Mundra today, sources said.
They believe the newcomer wants to assess market response before deciding to add more ships for a fixed schedule rotation, either fortnightly or weekly.
They see the intended coverage as a strategic move by JPL, as trades exposed to operational and security risks typically offer potential for higher freight yields.
According to the latest India-Middle East price index from Container Trades Statistics, freight rates have soared this year following the outbreak of conflict, eschewing the stability seen in 2025 – its August price index was up more than 250% year on year.
Source: Container Trades Statistics
“Regional shipping networks are not shaped only by the largest global carriers,” said Sean Fang, senior consultant at China-based Way-Way International Logistics.
“Smaller operators can also create additional links between specific origin and destination markets, particularly where regional cargo demand supports a more-focused service.” he added in a media post.
Capacity released by SeaLead had largely been captured by emerging Chinese liner CULines, which has consolidated regional operations alongside the predominant intra-Asia regional carriers.
Signalling its growth plans, CULines has swiftly expanded its fleet to more than 50 containerships, and recently signed a major order for two 14,000 teu newbuildings at China’s Hudong-Zhonghua Shipbuilding.
The wider intra-Asia trades are undoubtedly crowded with carriers, but their underlying resilient demand strengths continue to attract capacity participants.
While the region’s core growth appeal lies in the concentration of production centres, accelerating supply chain diversification, the region is delivering another source of intra-regional cargo opportunities for ocean capacity stakeholders, industry experts believe.

AI and digital fluency rank among the most needed procurement skills for 2030, but few leaders believe their teams are prepared for future demands, according to new research from Procurious . The report found that 82% identify AI and digital fluency as a priority, while only 28% say their teams are ready for what lies ahead.
What’s Related
The findings also show that training is struggling to keep pace. More than half of procurement teams have no structured, future-focused training plan, and 66% of respondents say their training budget is insufficient.
The report found that more than 90% of respondents say skills shortages already affect their ability to meet business objectives. Those concerns extend beyond learning how to use new technology to the commercial decisions procurement teams make.
“Closing the gap requires more than static curricula and occasional training,” said Tania Seary, founder of Procurious.
RELATED STORIES: Procurement Has Big AI Plans. Its Data Isn’t Ready | AI Is Reshaping Procurement Jobs, But Few Leaders Have Redesigned Them
Skills beyond AI
After AI and digital fluency, respondents identified working with and influencing people across the business (42%) and commercial judgement (39%) as priority skills for 2030. Those findings point to the importance of skills that extend beyond using technology.
“Procurement is a profession built on relationships, judgement and influence,” said Jade Cusworth, global learning and development director at Procurious+. “People develop those by pulling in outside expertise, working through real problems and comparing notes with peers who are facing the same ones.”
Respondents also pointed to consequences if skills shortages remain unaddressed over the next 12 to 24 months:
Compliance : 30% say regulatory compliance and efforts to reduce audit risk would suffer.
Revenue: 22% point to effects on outcomes such as time to market and supplier innovation .
Supply disruptions : 21% say disruptions would become harder to manage.
The concerns were more pronounced at larger businesses. Among respondents at companies with more than $5 billion in revenue, 45% say skills shortages create noticeable or significant challenges, compared with 36% overall.
No budget, no time
Nearly 60% of respondents lack a formal framework defining the procurement skills their teams need. More than half lack either the budget or the time and resources to develop and maintain training programs.
Even when training is available, people struggle to find time to participate. Workload prevents 52% of respondents from actively taking part in development opportunities.
Spending is uneven, too: 9% report investing nothing per employee, and 40% have no defined per-employee training budget. When asked what spending should be, 36% favor $2,000 or more, while another 21% favor $1,500 to $2,000.
Procurious founder Tania Seary said businesses need to commit resources to developing procurement teams as their responsibilities grow. “Procurement can't build that capability on its own. The business has to put time and money behind it.”

Danish freight forwarder Scan Global Logistics (SGL) is set to undertake its largest takeover, agreeing to acquire its US counterpart, OIA Global, in a deal expected to propel SGL into the ranks of the world’s 20 largest freight forwarders.
“The acquisition of OIA Global marks a significant milestone for Scan Global Logistics. As our largest investment to date, it will place us among the world’s top 20 freight forwarders, strengthen our position in key markets, and expand our capabilities across the supply chain,” said CEO Allan Melgaard.
“Together with OIA Global’s talented people and experienced leadership team, we will create a stronger, more resilient platform for future growth,” he added.
News of the deal was first flagged on Loadstar Premium’s DeskOne news feed yesterday:
Source: DeskOne
While the purchase price was undisclosed, SGL has spent much of the past month raising funds, and on 22 October successfully issued a €300m bond, which it said would be partly used to finance its next acquisition.
Meanwhile, The Loadstar also understands that SGL’s shareholders, led by private equity firm CVC Capital Partners, have injected a further €111m to help fund the deal.
According to SGL, OIA Global posted revenues of $780m in 2025, and employs around 1,200 staff across 60 offices.
According to The Loadstar’s sources in the M&A field, OIA Global has been on the market for some time – the US family-owned fund Lacy Diversified Industries (LDI) seeking an exit.
LDI acquired OIA in 2010 and since has completed five acquisitions to expand OIA’s geographic and vertical scope – the first of which was the purchase of UK forwarder Belville Rodair in 2013, which gave it its first presence in Europe.
“What stood out to us about Scan Global Logistics was not only the scale of the organisation, but also the way it does business,” said OIA Global CEO Jeffery Barrie. “Both companies are built on strong customer relationships, entrepreneurial thinking, and empowered local teams.
“These shared values provide a strong foundation for the future and make SGL the right partner for OIA Global,” he added.
SGL added: “OIA has developed a diversified business model that extends beyond traditional freight forwarding. Its established capabilities in supply chain management, customs brokerage, project logistics, and packaging solutions will complement SGL’s expertise and broaden the combined company’s ability to support customers across increasingly complex global supply chains.”
The deal is expected to close in the first quarter of next year.
